subject: seasons
title: Seasons: Geometry Beats Distance
summary: Insolation geometry, the 6.8% January bonus, and why tilt drives ice ages.

keys.prompt: Why does angle beat distance for seasons?
keys.answer: At 30° elevation a beam covers twice the area it would overhead (half the energy per square meter); distance changes sunlight only about 6.8%.

keys.prompt: What does Earth's eccentricity actually do?
keys.answer: A second-order effect: about 6.8% more sunlight in January, and Northern summers about 4.5 days longer than winters.

keys.prompt: How does lower axial tilt help ice sheets grow?
keys.answer: Milder summers at high latitudes let snow persist from year to year.

cards.title: The 6.8% puzzle
cards.text: Each January, Earth receives about 6.8% more incoming sunlight than in July, because it is about 3.2 million miles closer to the Sun. Yet January is the Northern Hemisphere's winter. What dominates, and by how much?

cards.question: At 30° solar elevation, how much energy does each square meter of ground get compared with the Sun overhead?
cards.reveal: About half: the beam covers twice the area. That swing in angle dwarfs the ~6.8% sunlight difference from distance.

cards.title: Geometry first
cards.text: Earth's axis is tilted 23.4° to its orbital plane and keeps a fixed orientation in space, so the subsolar latitude swings through the year. Energy per unit of ground area scales roughly with the sine of the Sun's elevation: at 30°, a beam covers twice the area it would overhead.

cards.title: Distance is a second-order term
cards.text: Perihelion comes around January 3 and aphelion around July 4, a 3.4% variation in distance and about 6.8% in sunlight. That is real, but small next to the swing in sun angle at mid-latitudes. Eccentricity does make Northern summers about 4.5 days longer than Northern winters.

cards.title: Tilt on long timescales
cards.text: Tilt (obliquity) has varied between 22.1° and 24.5° over the last million years on a cycle of about 41,000 years. It is about 23.4° now and slowly decreasing. Larger tilt means more extreme seasons. Lower tilt gives milder summers that, at high latitudes, let snow persist and ice sheets build.
cards.example: NASA notes that the relative importance of tilt versus precession for ice ages is still being studied.

why.q: Why would milder summers, not colder winters, build ice sheets?
why.a: Ice builds when summer fails to melt the winter's snow. Milder summers let snow persist year to year.

cards.title: Origin
cards.text: NASA Space Place notes scientists think an impact with a body called Theia knocked the young Earth off-kilter, and most think the debris formed the Moon.

cards.prompt: In "Rayleigh's Sky: A Model That Predicts," path length explained sunsets better than the source. Here, angle beats distance. What's the common lesson?
cards.model: Geometry (path and angle) dominates the intuitive cause; the easy-to-see variable is second-order.

cards.question: "Closer is hotter" is intuitive and wrong for seasons, because a first-order variable (angle) swamps a second-order one (distance). Where in your work do people over-attribute outcomes to the variable that is easiest to see?
nudges: Rank the drivers of a metric you manage by actual sensitivity.

questions.q: About how much more sunlight reaches Earth at perihelion (January) than at aphelion (July)?

options.why: From a 3.4% distance variation (inverse-square roughly doubles it).
That is the figure at maximum orbital eccentricity, not today.

questions.q: Over the last million years, Earth's tilt has ranged between…

options.why: On a cycle of about 41,000 years.
Far wider than the actual range.

questions.q: Why do Northern Hemisphere summers last about 4.5 days longer than winters?

options.text: Orbital eccentricity: Earth moves slower near aphelion in July.
options.why: Eccentricity changes season lengths, even though tilt drives the seasons.
Tilt doesn't change within a year.
A clock convention, not orbital mechanics.
Not the cause given by NASA.

video.title: Reasons for the seasons - Rebecca Kaplan
video.why: Why distance from the sun isn't the cause — we're closest in January — and how tilt drives the seasons.

sources.title: What Causes the Seasons?
sources.supports: Tilt, not distance, causes seasons; the tilted axis keeps pointing the same way; June and December; perihelion (91.4 million miles) in January and aphelion (94.5 million miles) in July; the Theia impact idea.

sources.title: Earth: Facts
sources.supports: Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to its orbit, and this tilt causes the yearly cycle of seasons.

sources.title: Milankovitch (Orbital) Cycles and Their Role in Earth's Climate
sources.supports: Tilt has ranged from 22.1 to 24.5 degrees over the last million years on a roughly 41,000-year cycle; perihelion about January 3 brings about 6.8% more sunlight than aphelion; Northern summers are about 4.5 days longer than winters.
